title: Bridging or Breaking: Impact of Intergroup Interactions on Religious Polarization
benchmark_measurement: The study measures religious polarization by introducing a new metric called the Group Conformity Score (GCS). GCS quantifies how similar an individual's tweets are to the discourse of their own religious group versus that of another religious group, based on contextualized text embeddings. The core analysis measures the change in GCS following intergroup interactions on Twitter during specific real-world events.
base_benchmarks: leave-out estimator of phrase partisanship (Gentzkow et al., 2019)
findings: The study found that intergroup interactions on Twitter generally reduce religious polarization, particularly during political and social events. However, this effect is weaker for individuals who already exhibit high conformity to their group. In contrast, during communal events, intergroup interactions can exacerbate polarization and increase group conformity, especially for the minority (Muslim) group. The dynamics of religious polarization are highly sensitive to the context of the event.
